newsitem.title: USA: Mississippi night hazardous loads face likely ban.
newsitem.headline: Mississippi night hazardous loads face likely ban.

text.p: The Coast Guard is likely to announce Thursday or Friday new regulations preventing night shipments of "hazardous cargoes" on the swollen Mississippi River until dangerous currents subside, a senior Coast Guard officer said.

"The river is unusually fast with a number of barge breakaways and collisions. We've been lucky so far that nobody has been killed," said Chief Petty Officer Neal Powell at the Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in New Orleans.
He said it would affect mainly petroleum products and chemicals carried by vessels of 1,600 gross tons or more.
"The regulations would probably be (issued) at the end of the day or on Friday...(and) I support them," Powell said.

He added that the regulations are expected following days of discussions between Coast Guard officials and Louisiana Governor Murphy J. "Mike" Foster, who said Tuesday he would push for a ban on shipments of barges carrying toxic chemicals.

Foster also said on Tuesday that he had warned large industry along the river of a possible ban on traffic if conditions became too hazardous. But both the Coast Guard and Foster's office said Wednesday that every effort would be made to avoid a full-scale ban because of the impact to local economies all along the Mississippi.
According to the recent government figures, approximately 66.50 million tons of crude and petroleum products cargoes travel annually from the mouth of the river to Minneapolis, Minnesota.

Swift currents have been linked to a series of highly publicized river accidents in recent weeks. On March 17 a barge capsized after its tow hit the U.S. 190 bridge in Baton Rouge, spilling a liquid hydrocarbon containing toxic benzene.
And rushing currents are suspected to have rammed debris into a 10-inch natural gas pipeline Tuesday in West Baton Rouge Parish, rupturing the Cypress Pipeline Co line.

"Any tank vessel or tank ship 1,600 gross tons or more carrying certain oils and chemicals would only be able to operate in the daytime" under the expected regulations, Powell said. "The effect would mainly be on petroleum products and chemicals."
Powell said the river is at its highest point since 1983 and is expected to remain a serious navigational threat for at least another four or five days.
"The Coast Guard has many concerns, including the possibility a vessel could punch a hole in a levee and flood a community," Powell said.
He noted the Mississippi's elevation at New Orleans is at a precarious 16.8 to 16.9 feet -- just shy of the official flood stage of 17.0 feet.
Powell said potential floodwaters had been siphoned away on March 17 when officials opened the Bonnet Carre spillway just north of New Orleans, diverting some waters into nearby Lake Pontchartrain.

The night travel ban would be in addition to other recent restrictions placed on traffic by the Coast Guard. Fleet operators have been told to restrict their loads to 25 barges per 747 horsepower on the tugs, or about half the usual load. Also, the Coast Guard has asked that barges containing hazardous loads be in the middle of barge chains rather than at the end.

The Louisiana governor, while wanting to avoid disruption to commerce along the river, would apply pressure for further restrictions if there was another accident involving hazardous material, according to Foster's spokesperson.
"He doesn't really want to have to shut the river and there are a lot of things to consider but safety is first," said Marsanne Golsby, Foster's press secretary.

"I can say with confidence, if there are any more serious accidents on the river he would put the request (for the river to be closed) in the strongest terms. And I can't imagine that if the governor asked them in really strong terms that (the Coast Guard) would say 'no,'" Golsby added.

On Wednesday, five state office buildings and schools near the governor's office in Baton Rouge, Louisiana were evacuated by Louisiana State Police after some people located near the capsized barge containing benzene complained of dizziness and blurry vision.
--((Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk, +1 212 859 1632))
